title: The Day the River Flooded
summary: A farm family races to move their animals to higher ground when a sudden flood strikes, and their neighbors help them recover afterward.
poll: Communities only truly come together to help each other after something bad, like a flood, happens.

versions.title: The Day the River Flooded
versions.text:
Sara and Yousef live on a farm. The farm is next to a river. They have sheep. They have a cow. They have chickens, too.

It rains a lot one week. The river gets big. Father looks at the river. He feels worried.

One day the rain does not stop. The river gets too big. Water comes into the field! Father calls to the family. "Wake up! We must move fast!" he says.

Sara and Yousef help. They walk the sheep up the hill. They walk the cow up, too. Mother carries the chickens. Father carries bags of food.

They all get to the high ground. They are safe now. They watch the flood from the hill. The water covers the field below.

The next day, the rain stops. The water goes down. Mud is on the ground. Neighbors come to help. They clean the mud. They fix the fence. They share food with the family.

Sara and Yousef are happy. Their neighbors are kind. The farm will be good again soon.

Sara and her brother Yousef live on a small farm. The farm is next to a wide river. They have sheep, a cow, and chickens.

Every year, rain falls for many days. This year, the rain falls harder. The river slowly gets bigger. Their father checks the river each morning. He feels a little worried.

One night, the rain does not stop. The river rises fast. Water comes into the field! Father calls to the family. "Wake up! We must move fast!" he says.

Sara and Yousef jump up to help. They walk the sheep up the hill. They walk the cow up, too. Mother carries the chickens in a basket. Father carries food and blankets.

The family reaches the high ground. They are safe. They watch the flood below. Brown water covers the field.

By morning, the rain stops. The water goes down. Thick mud covers the ground. Neighbors come to help. They clean the mud. They fix the fence. They share warm food.

Sara and Yousef feel happy. Their neighbors are kind. The farm will be good again soon.

versions.title: The Day the River Flooded
versions.text:
Sara and her younger brother Yousef live on a small farm. Their farm is next to a wide river. The family has sheep, a cow, and chickens.

Every year, the rainy season brings days of rain. This year, the rain falls harder and longer. The river grows wider. Each morning their father checks the water. Each day he looks more worried.

Then, one dark night, the rain does not stop. The river rises fast. Cold water creeps into the lower field. Father bursts into the house. "Wake up, everyone!" he shouts. "The flood is coming fast. We must move now!"

Sara and Yousef jump out of bed to help. They carry food and blankets outside. They guide the sheep up the hillside path. Yousef leads the cow slowly, speaking softly so she stays calm. Mother carries the chickens in a basket.

At last, the family reaches the high ground. They are safe. They turn to watch. Thick, brown flood water covers the field and the garden below.

By early morning, the rain eases. Slowly the water drains away. It leaves mud and branches everywhere. Soon, kind neighbors arrive with shovels and buckets. Together they scrape away the mud, mend the fence, and share warm bread and tea.

Sara and Yousef feel grateful. Their neighbors' kindness shows how strong a community can be. Soon their farm will be busy again.

versions.title: The Day the River Flooded
versions.text:
Sara and her younger brother Yousef live on a small farm beside a wide river. Their family raises sheep, a dairy cow, and a dozen chickens.

Every year the rainy season brings days of steady rain. This year the rain falls harder and lasts much longer than before. The river grows wider and faster. Each morning their father checks the rising water. Each day his face looks more worried.

Then, on one dark and stormy night, the rain does not stop at all. The river rises fast. Cold, muddy water creeps into the lower field. Father bursts through the door. "Wake up, everyone!" he shouts. "The flood is coming fast. We have to move now, before it is too late!"

Sara and Yousef leap out of bed to help. They carry boxes of food and blankets outside. They guide the frightened sheep along the narrow path up the hill. Yousef leads the cow slowly behind them, speaking softly so she stays calm. Mother carries the squawking chickens in a large basket.

At last the family reaches the high ground, safe from the rising water. They turn and watch the flood rise below. Thick, brown water spreads across the field, covering the fences, the garden, and the small wooden shed.

By early next morning, the rain eases. Slowly the flood water drains back toward the river. It leaves deep mud, branches, and a strong, damp smell. Soon kind neighbors arrive with shovels, buckets, and supplies. Together everyone scrapes away the mud, repairs the fence, and shares warm bread, tea, and dates with the tired family.

Sara and Yousef feel deeply grateful. Their neighbors' kindness shows how strong a caring community can be. Soon their farm will be green and busy again.

versions.title: The Day the River Flooded
versions.text:
Sara and her younger brother, Yousef, lived on a small farm beside a wide river. Their family cared for sheep, a dairy cow, and a dozen chickens.

Every year the rainy season brought days of steady rain. This year the rain fell harder. It lasted much longer than before. Little by little the river grew wider and swifter. Each morning their father walked down to check the rising water. Each day his face looked more worried. He had lived near this river his whole life. Something about its rise worried him more than usual.

Then, on one dark and stormy night, the rain refused to stop. The river, usually no deeper than a person's waist, rose nearly two meters in one night. Cold, muddy water came rushing into the lower field. Father burst through the door. He shouted that the family needed to evacuate the lower farm right away, before the water reached the house.

Sara and Yousef leapt out of bed to help move the livestock to safety. They guided the frightened sheep along the narrow path up the hill. Yousef led the cow slowly behind them. He spoke calmly so she would not panic in the rushing water. Mother herded the squawking chickens into a basket. Father rushed to gather food, blankets, and important papers.

At last the family reached the high ground, safe at last. They turned and watched the flood rise below. Thick, brown water spread across the field. It covered the fences, the garden, and the small wooden shed near the barn.

By early morning, the rain eased. Slowly the floodwater drained back toward the river. It left deep mud, scattered debris, and a strong, damp smell. Soon kind neighbors arrived with shovels, buckets, and supplies. Together everyone scraped away the mud, repaired the fence, and shared warm bread, tea, and dates with the tired family.

Sara and Yousef felt deeply grateful for their neighbors' kindness. It showed just how strong a caring community could be in hard times. Within a few weeks, with everyone's help, the family began to recover. The farm slowly grew green and busy again.

versions.title: The Night the River Rose
versions.text:
Sara and her younger brother, Yousef, lived on a modest farm beside a wide river at the edge of their village, where their family tended sheep, a dairy cow, and a dozen chickens. Every year the rainy season brought days of steady rain, but this year the rain fell harder and lasted much longer than anyone expected.

Little by little the river grew wider and swifter as the days passed, since rivers often rise fastest during such storms: rain falling on hills far upstream flows down into the same channel, adding more water than the ground can soak up. Each morning their father walked down to check the rising water, and each day his face looked more worried, for he had lived near this river his whole life and understood its moods well.

Then, on one dark and stormy night, the rain refused to stop at all. The river, usually no deeper than a person's waist, surged nearly two meters in a single night, overtopping the low earthen embankment and sending a torrent of cold, muddy water rushing into the lower field. Father burst through the door and shouted that the family needed to evacuate the lower farm right away, before the surging water reached the house.

Sara and Yousef leapt out of bed and hurried outside to help move the livestock to higher, safer ground. They guided the frightened sheep along the narrow, slippery path up the hill, while Yousef led the cow slowly behind them, speaking calmly so she would not panic in the rushing torrent. Mother herded the squawking chickens into a basket, while father rushed to gather food, blankets, and important papers before the water could reach them.

At last the family reached the safety of the high ground, breathing hard from the climb. They turned back and watched the flood rise below them, the torrent spreading across the whole field and covering the fences, the garden, and the small wooden shed.

By early the next morning, the rain eased, and slowly the floodwater drained back past the broken embankment toward the river, leaving behind deep mud, scattered debris, and a strong, damp smell. Soon, resilient neighbors arrived carrying shovels, buckets, and supplies to help with the cleanup. Together everyone scraped away the mud, repaired the fence, and shared warm bread, tea, and dates with the tired family.

Sara and Yousef felt deeply grateful for their neighbors' kindness, which showed just how resilient a caring community could be in hard times. Within a few weeks, the family worked steadily to restore their farm, and it slowly grew green and busy again.

versions.title: The Night the River Rose
versions.text:
Sara and her younger brother, Yousef, resided on a modest farm situated beside a wide, generally placid river at the edge of their village, where their family tended a flock of sheep, a gentle dairy cow, and a dozen chickens. Each year, the rainy season brought several days of steady rainfall, but that particular year the rain fell with unusual intensity and persisted considerably longer than anyone in the family had ever anticipated.

Gradually, the river swelled wider and swifter as the days wore on, since rivers typically rise most rapidly during such prolonged storms: precipitation falling across the hills far upstream flows downward into the same channel, delivering substantially more water than the parched ground is capable of absorbing. Each morning, their father walked down to the riverbank to assess the steadily rising water, and each morning his expression grew visibly more concerned than it had been the previous day, for he had resided beside this river his entire life and understood its unpredictable moods intimately.

Then, on one dark and tempestuous night, the rain refused to relent even momentarily. The river, ordinarily no deeper than a person's waist, surged nearly two meters within a single night, overtopping its low earthen embankment entirely, and a powerful torrent of cold, muddy water came rushing into the lower field surrounding the house. Their father burst through the door, shouting urgently that the family needed to evacuate the lower farm immediately, before the surging water could reach the house itself.

Sara and Yousef leapt from their beds and hurried outside to assist in moving the livestock to higher, more secure ground. Working quickly and efficiently as a coordinated team, they guided the frightened sheep along the narrow, slippery path leading up the hillside. Yousef led the cow slowly behind them, speaking in a calm, steady voice so that she would not panic amid the rushing torrent swirling around her legs. Meanwhile, their mother herded the squawking chickens into a large woven basket, while their father rushed to gather boxes of food, blankets, and important family documents before the rising water could reach them.

At last, the whole family reached the safety of the elevated ground, breathing hard from the exertion of the steep climb. Turning back, they watched the flood rise relentlessly below them in the darkness, the torrent spreading across the entire lower field within mere minutes and swallowing the fences, the vegetable garden, and the small wooden shed standing near the barn.

By early the following morning, the rain finally eased, and slowly the floodwater began draining back past the breached embankment toward the riverbed. It left behind deep mud, scattered debris, and a strong, damp smell permeating the entire farm. Soon, remarkably resilient neighbors arrived carrying shovels, buckets, and extra supplies to lend assistance with the arduous cleanup. Together, everyone scraped away the thick mud, repaired the broken fence, and shared warm bread, tea, and dates with the exhausted family as they labored side by side throughout the day.

Sara and Yousef felt profoundly grateful for their neighbors' generous kindness, which reminded them precisely how resilient a genuinely caring community could prove during difficult times. Within a few weeks, with everyone contributing their effort, the family worked steadily to restore their farm completely, and it gradually grew green, busy, and full of life once again, emerging considerably stronger for having confronted the flood together as one united community.

Fish, turtles, and birds

wrong.A: These animals are not named in the story.
wrong.B: These animals are not named in the story.
wrong.D: These animals are not named in the story.

questions.stem: What did their father shout when the river rose fast?
options: Let's go fishing right now
Please feed the chickens first
Go back to sleep, it is fine
Wake up, we must move fast
questions.why: The father burst through the door and shouted that everyone must wake up and move fast.

wrong.A: The father was warning of danger, not inviting them to fish.
wrong.B: He was not worried about the chickens first.
wrong.C: He wanted everyone awake, not asleep.

questions.stem: Why did the family need to move the sheep and cow?
options: Floodwater was coming into the field
It was time for their yearly bath
The animals wanted to see the neighbors
The sun was too hot for them
questions.why: The rising river sent water into the lower field, so the family moved the animals to higher ground to keep them safe.

wrong.B: The story does not mention bathing the animals.
wrong.C: Animals do not choose to visit neighbors.
wrong.D: The flood happened at night during a storm, not from heat.

questions.stem: What happened after the family reached the high ground?
options: They went straight back to bed in the tent
They planted a new vegetable garden on the hill
They watched the flood cover the field below
They rode a boat across the river to town
questions.why: Once safe on the high ground, the family turned and watched the flood rise and cover the lower field.

wrong.A: They stayed awake watching the flood, not sleeping.
wrong.B: No gardening happens at that point in the story.
wrong.D: No boat is mentioned in the story.

questions.stem: Why did their father check the river every morning?
options: He liked to count the fish in it
He was worried that it might flood
He wanted to wash the sheep there
He was waiting for a boat to arrive
questions.why: The father watched the rising river with a worried face, which shows he feared it might flood.

wrong.A: Counting fish is not mentioned in the story.
wrong.C: Washing sheep is not mentioned in the story.
wrong.D: No boat is mentioned in the story.

questions.stem: In the story, the word carry means —
options: to throw something far away
to wash something very clean
to break something into parts
to hold something and move it
questions.why: The mother and father carry chickens and boxes, meaning they hold and move them to safety.

questions.stem: Why does the author tell about the neighbors helping after the flood?
options: To show how kind and helpful a community can be
To explain the steps to build a fence around a farm
To describe a recipe for warm bread in the oven
To show the family did not need any help at all
questions.why: The neighbors bring tools and food and work together, showing how a caring community helps in hard times.

wrong.B: The story does not give fence-building steps.
wrong.C: The story does not give a bread recipe.
wrong.D: The family needed and received a lot of help.

LOW.prompt: Do you think Sara and Yousef's family handled the flood well? Use at least two facts from the story to explain your answer.
checklist: I clearly said what I think.
I used at least two facts from the story.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
LOW.modelAnswer: I think Sara and Yousef's family handled the flood very well. When the water started to rise, they moved the sheep and the cow to high ground right away. They also worked together as a team, and their neighbors came to help clean up after the flood. This showed me that the family was smart and brave.

keyWords.definition: to move or do something very quickly
keyWords.example: The students rushed to get out of the rain.

keyWords.definition: farm animals such as cows, sheep, or chickens that are raised for food or work
keyWords.example: The farmer kept his livestock in a large barn.

keyWords.definition: to leave a dangerous place quickly to reach safety
keyWords.example: The town had to evacuate before the big storm arrived.

keyWords.definition: broken pieces of things left scattered after damage or a disaster
keyWords.example: Workers cleared the debris from the street after the storm.

keyWords.definition: to get back to a normal or healthy condition after a hard time
keyWords.example: It took the village many weeks to recover after the earthquake.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the story?
options: A family evacuates its livestock during a flood and recovers with help from neighbors.
A family moves to a new farm because they dislike heavy rain in their old home.
Neighbors in the village refuse to help each other in hard times, even during a flood.
The story mainly explains how to build a taller river embankment with stones and soil.
questions.why: The story follows the family's effort to evacuate their animals safely and the neighbors' help afterward, which is the main idea.

wrong.B: The family does not move away; they stay and rebuild.
wrong.C: The neighbors help a great deal in the story.
wrong.D: The story is a narrative, not instructions for building anything.

questions.stem: About how much did the river rise in a single night?
options: Only about ten centimeters
Exactly one kilometer wide
Nearly two meters
It did not rise at all that night
questions.why: The story states the river, normally no deeper than a person's waist, rose nearly two meters in a single night.

wrong.A: This is far too small a rise for the story's events.
wrong.B: A kilometer is a measure of distance, not depth.
wrong.D: The river rose dramatically that night.

questions.stem: What did the mother do to help during the flood?
options: She drove the family's old car into town
She herded the chickens into a large basket
She called the neighbors on the telephone
She stayed asleep inside the farmhouse
questions.why: The story says the mother gathered the chickens into a large basket while the father collected supplies.

wrong.A: No car is mentioned in the story.
wrong.D: She was awake and actively helping, not asleep.

questions.stem: Why did the river rise so quickly that stormy night?
options: The family had forgotten to close a gate near the old barn
The farm's chickens had dug a hole near the riverbank
The neighbors had opened a dam somewhere further upstream
Heavy rain upstream added more water than the ground could absorb
questions.why: The story explains that rain falling across hills upstream flows into the same channel, adding more water than the ground can absorb.

wrong.A: A gate is not mentioned in the story.
wrong.C: No dam is mentioned in the story.

questions.stem: In the story, the word evacuate means —
options: to leave a dangerous place quickly and reach safety
to construct a brand-new house very quickly indeed
to feed all of the farm animals every single morning
to carefully repair a broken wooden fence post
questions.why: The father shouted that the family needed to evacuate the lower farm, meaning they had to leave quickly for safety.

wrong.B: Evacuate does not mean building a house.
wrong.C: Evacuate does not mean feeding animals.
wrong.D: Evacuate does not mean repairing a fence.

questions.stem: Why did Yousef speak to the cow in a calm, steady voice?
options: He was practicing his lines for a school play
He wanted the cow to walk faster than the sheep
He hoped a calm voice would soothe the frightened cow
He was teaching the cow some new words
questions.why: Yousef spoke calmly to the cow in the rushing water so she would stay calm instead of panicking.

wrong.A: No play is mentioned in the story.
wrong.B: Speed is not why he used a calm voice.

questions.stem: What happened right before the neighbors arrived to help?
options: The father built a new, taller embankment overnight
The rain eased and the floodwater began draining away
The sheep ran back down into the flooded field
The family planted a new vegetable garden
questions.why: The story says the rain eased and the water began draining away, and soon after, the neighbors arrived to help.

wrong.A: No overnight embankment building is mentioned.
wrong.C: The sheep stayed safely on the high ground.
wrong.D: Planting happens later, not right before the neighbors arrive.

questions.stem: How does the author mainly organize the story?
options: By comparing two completely different farms in two separate countries
By listing numbered steps for cleaning up after any storm
By describing each farm animal one at a time with no real story
By following events in time order, from rain to recovery
questions.why: The story moves in time order: the rain begins, the river rises, the family evacuates, and the community helps them recover.

wrong.A: Only one farm is described in the story.
wrong.B: The story is a narrative, not a numbered list.
wrong.C: The animals are part of a connected story, not separate descriptions.

MID.prompt: Explain how the family and their neighbors worked together before and after the flood. Use at least two details from the story.
checklist: I explained how the family acted during the flood.
I explained how the neighbors helped after the flood.
I used at least two details from the story.
MID.modelAnswer: Before the flood got worse, Sara, Yousef, and their parents worked together quickly to move the sheep, the cow, and the chickens to higher ground, along with important food and papers. After the flood, their neighbors arrived with shovels and buckets to help clear away the mud and debris, repair the broken fence, and share food with the tired family. Because everyone helped, the farm began to recover within a few weeks.

keyWords.definition: a very strong, fast-moving flow of water
keyWords.example: A torrent of rainwater rushed down the mountain road.

keyWords.definition: a raised bank of earth or stone built to hold back water or support a road
keyWords.example: Workers built a tall embankment to protect the village from the river.

keyWords.definition: to increase or rush forward suddenly and powerfully, especially of water
keyWords.example: A surge of seawater flooded the harbor during the storm.

keyWords.definition: able to recover quickly from difficulty or damage
keyWords.example: The small village proved resilient after the earthquake and rebuilt within a year.

keyWords.definition: to bring something back to its earlier, good condition
keyWords.example: Volunteers worked for months to restore the old library after the fire.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the story?
options: The family's quick thinking and a resilient community help them survive the flood and rebuild.
A family abandons their farm forever after just one bad flood, and the village is empty.
The story mainly explains how to measure a river's exact depth with a rope and stone.
A family builds an embankment that stops every future flood completely, and no flood ever comes.
questions.why: The story centers on the family's quick response to the flood and the resilient community that helps them restore their farm afterward.

wrong.B: The family stays and rebuilds rather than abandoning the farm.
wrong.C: The story does not argue against living near rivers in general.
wrong.D: The embankment is overtopped, not a permanent solution.

questions.stem: Why did the river overtop its embankment so suddenly?
options: The embankment had never actually been built at all
The family had removed the embankment themselves before the storm
Chickens had weakened the embankment by digging underneath it
An intense storm sent more water downstream than the ground could absorb
questions.why: The story explains that an intense, prolonged storm sent far more water downstream than the ground could absorb, causing the river to surge and overtop the embankment.

wrong.A: The embankment existed before it was overtopped.
wrong.B: The family did not remove any embankment.
wrong.C: Chickens digging is not mentioned in the story.

questions.stem: What evidence in the story shows the father's long experience with the river?
options: He had never seen the river before that stormy night
He had lived beside the river his entire life and knew its moods
He read about the river's history in a book that morning
A neighbor warned him about the river for the very first time
questions.why: The story says he had lived near the river his entire life and understood its unpredictable moods intimately.

wrong.A: He had lived there his whole life, not just one night.
wrong.C: No book is mentioned in the story.
wrong.D: He already understood the river without a neighbor's first warning.

questions.stem: In the story, the word resilient most nearly means —
options: unable to recover from any kind of damage
afraid of difficult or dangerous situations
able to recover quickly from hardship or damage
slow and hesitant to respond to danger
questions.why: The story describes the neighbors and community as resilient, meaning they recover quickly and work hard despite the hardship of the flood.

wrong.A: This is the opposite of resilient.
wrong.B: The neighbors act bravely, not fearfully.
wrong.D: The neighbors respond quickly, not slowly.

questions.stem: What can readers infer about the family from how quickly they reacted to the rising water?
options: They had likely planned beforehand what to do if the river flooded
They had never once considered the river dangerous before
They wanted an excuse to leave the farm permanently and move away
They did not care much about their animals' safety at all
questions.why: Their calm, organized, and fast response suggests the family had some sense of what to do if the river ever flooded.

wrong.B: Their quick, organized reaction suggests real concern about the river.
wrong.C: The family works hard to stay and rebuild, not to leave.
wrong.D: They worked hard specifically to save their animals.

questions.stem: Put these events in the order they happened.
options: Neighbors arrived to help, the embankment overtopped, the family evacuated
The embankment overtopped, the family evacuated, neighbors arrived to help
The family evacuated, neighbors arrived to help, the embankment overtopped
The family evacuated, the embankment overtopped, neighbors arrived to help
questions.why: The embankment was overtopped first, which forced the family to evacuate, and only afterward did the neighbors arrive to help clean up.

wrong.C: The embankment overtopped before the family evacuated, not after.
wrong.D: The family evacuated because the embankment overtopped, not before it.

questions.stem: Why does the author include the detail that the river was "ordinarily no deeper than a person's waist"?
options: To teach readers how to measure a river's depth accurately
To suggest that the river was never truly dangerous at all
To emphasize how extraordinary and dangerous the sudden rise truly was
To compare the river to an ordinary swimming pool at a big hotel in town
questions.why: Comparing the river's normal depth to its sudden two-meter rise highlights just how extreme and dangerous that night's flood really was.

wrong.A: This is not a lesson on measuring rivers.
wrong.B: The detail shows the river became very dangerous.
wrong.D: The comparison is about depth, not about swimming pools.

questions.stem: How are Sara and Yousef's roles during the flood similar?
options: Both children act quickly and calmly to help move the livestock to safety
Both children refuse to help move any of the farm animals
Both children spend the night searching anxiously for their parents
Both children care more about saving toys than saving animals
questions.why: Both Sara and Yousef immediately get up and work calmly and quickly to guide the sheep and cow to higher ground.

wrong.B: Both children actively help move the animals.
wrong.C: Their parents are present and working alongside them.
wrong.D: No toys are mentioned; both children focus on the animals.

HIGH.prompt: The poll might claim that nothing good can come from a disaster like a flood. Do you agree or disagree? Support your argument with evidence from the story about the family's preparation, their response, and their community's help.
checklist: I supported my position with specific evidence from the story.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I disagree that nothing good can come from a disaster like a flood. Although the flood in the story was frightening and destroyed part of the farm, it also revealed how resilient and generous the family's community truly was: neighbors arrived with shovels and supplies to help clean up, repair the fence, and share food. Someone might argue that the flood only caused loss and should never be seen as positive, but the story shows that facing hardship together helped the family and their neighbors grow closer and more prepared for the future, which is a meaningful kind of good.
